title: JD Vance Just Dropped a Book That Has Democrats Terrified About 2028
text:
Peter Thiel walked into a lecture hall in Silicon Valley and said something JD Vance never forgot.
JD Vance just published a book about finding God – and it may be the most important thing he's ever written.
Read what Vance admitted about the moment that shattered his atheism, and you'll understand why Democrats are already in panic mode.
From Hillbilly to the Vice Presidency – With a Stop at Atheism Hillbilly Elegy made JD Vance a national figure in 2016 by explaining Trump's America to the coastal elites who couldn't understand it.
Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith , out today, tells a different story – the one that comes after the hillbilly kid from Appalachia graduated from Yale, worked in finance, and discovered that success felt like nothing.
https://twitter.com/FoxNews_Flash/status/2066190203656802587?s=20
Vance traces his journey from childhood Christianity through a cold, deliberate atheism he embraced after his grandmother – his mamaw – died.
"With her gone, no one really cared about my faith, and soon I stopped caring, too," he wrote.
He found a replacement for God in Ayn Rand.
Rand's philosophy of rational self-interest appealed to the newly successful version of Vance – thriving professionally, feeling zero pull toward anything larger than himself.
"I didn't care about God's will," he wrote. "I cared about my own."
That worked fine until Vance walked into a Peter Thiel lecture.
The Moment Peter Thiel Broke JD Vance's Atheism Thiel – the PayPal billionaire who would later become one of Vance's earliest political backers – was talking about hypercompetition among professionals and what he saw as technological stagnation.
Vance had built a neat mental model: smart people were atheists, religious people were intellectually soft.
https://twitter.com/NewsTongueX/status/2066166816741732729?s=20
Thiel demolished it in one sentence.
"Possibly the smartest person I'd ever met, he identified very openly as a Christian," Vance wrote.
That cracked the foundation – but it wasn't the moment Vance believed.
That came on a rain-slicked mountain road after his grandmother's funeral.
Returning to his military base, Vance lost control of his car – and then inexplicably stopped, just before hitting a guardrail and going over the side of a mountain.
He wrote it was "the closest I've ever come to a supernatural experience" – a feeling that stayed with him, he said, "even during my later years as a strident atheist."
The full conversion still took years – marriage to Usha, a visit to a French cathedral in 2018 where he felt what he called "a distinct sense of belonging and presence," and finally baptism into the Catholic Church in 2019.
He credits his faith with giving him something Yale and Wall Street never could: a sense of purpose.
Why This Book Is Coming Out Right Now Communion hits shelves less than five months before the 2026 midterm elections – the unofficial start of the 2028 race.
https://twitter.com/CBSSunday/status/2066160807952396449?s=20
Vance is the clear frontrunner for the Republican presidential nomination, polling at 36% among Republicans and right-leaning independents in a June 2026 Center Square poll – roughly double Rubio's support.
A Vance ally told CNN that Trump's team signed off on the book before it went to print – and welcomed it.
The Catholic Moment Is Real Here's what the media won't tell you: Vance isn't riding a niche trend.
He's surfing a wave.
Since around 2022, dioceses across the country have reported a surge in adult conversions – and the people walking through the doors are young, with men under 35 leading the charge.
Some archdioceses recorded their highest number of new Catholics in two decades this past Easter.
The Diocese of Cleveland saw conversions climb 49% in 2025 and the Archdiocese of Newark reports a 72% increase over the past three years.
https://twitter.com/China_hp1/status/2064175667634372766?s=20
A Vance candidacy built around faith, family, and American identity is going to land differently in 2028 than it would have in 2020.
What Democrats Are Missing Democrats keep looking for the standard Republican candidate – someone they can dismiss as a corporate tool or a culture warrior.
Vance doesn't fit either box.
He's the kid from Middletown, Ohio who escaped poverty, made it to Yale, served in the Marines, got famous explaining Trump America to people who hated it, and then found God in a French cathedral.
Communion puts that whole story in one place – and this one is written by a man who knows exactly where he's going.
The "childless cat ladies" comment was boneheaded – Vance says so himself in the book – but it was also the wrong battle at the right moment.
His actual argument, that America has become "pathologically hostile to having kids," is exactly what millions of Americans believe and nobody in Washington will say plainly.
That's the whole point of this book.
The kid who chased money and atheism and nearly drove off a mountain – and found his way home – just told the country who he is before the race starts.
Your 70-year-old grandmother who's been praying for this country for decades knows exactly what to make of that.

Rand's philosophy of rational self-interest appealed to the newly successful version of Vance – thriving professionally, feeling zero pull toward anything larger than himself.
